title: Restitution, Northward
spine: The briefing follows Postel's restitutio omnium through a four-letter Tarot, three Rosicrucian epochs, and Bureus's northern rune.

slides.title: Restitution, Northward
slides.subtitle: Postel, the four-letter Tarot, the Rose Cross, and the rune of the North.

slides.question: How does one doctrine of restitution travel from Postel into the Tarot, the Rose Cross, and the North?
slides.why: Each system in the briefing claims a single order: one restitution, one sacred name, one invisible fraternity, one northern king.
slides.notes: The deck selects. It does not transcribe the briefing. Biographical detail, the alphabet list, and the temple lore sit in later speaker notes.

slides.title: Six works the briefing uses

sources.title: Clavis, with Key of the Key

slides.notes: Also in the briefing, and not given a line here: Grammatica Arabica, about 1538; De Originibus, 1533/1538; Candelabri typici, 1548; the Zohar on Genesis and Sefer Yetzirah in Latin, 1552.

slides.title: Three offices, one scholar

items.label: Linguistic pioneer
items.note: Arabic grammar and twelve alphabets, both in 1538. A Semitic family.

items.label: Christian Kabbalist
items.note: First Latin Zohar on Genesis, and Sefer Yetzirah, in 1552.

items.label: Prophetic universalist
items.note: Restitutio omnium, under one Pan-Sophia and a world monarchy.

slides.notes: Postel, 25 March 1510 to 6 September 1581. François I sent him to Istanbul in 1536 with Jean de la Forest. Chair at the Collège Royal, 1538. He joined the Jesuits under Ignatius Loyola in 1544 and was expelled. The Roman Inquisition held him in Castel Sant'Angelo, 1555–1559. From 1563 he was confined at Saint Martin des Champs, where he taught Scaliger and Raphelengius and aided the Antwerp Polyglot.

slides.title: The New Eve, then the key
slides.evidence: In Venice, Postel met Mère Jeanne, called the mater mundi and the New Eve, a feminine spiritual messiah with a perfect Kabbalah.
slides.implication: After her death he claimed her spirit immuted into his body, and he took the name Elias Pandocheus.
slides.notes: He was censoring Hebrew print for Daniel Bomberg. She was about fifty, and uneducated. The Clavis of 1547 is the Key to all things hidden in the constitution of the World. The Menorah treatise, Candelabri typici, followed in 1548, after the Hebrew broadsheet Or Nerot ha-Menorah. His Hebrew style-name was Ish Kefar Sekhanya u-Shemo Eliyyahu Kol-Maskalyah.

slides.title: A path into the sanctuary

steps.label: Decrees of initiates
steps.note: Mercabah, the chariot, and the Sephirothic wheels.

steps.label: The sacred monotriad
steps.note: Three lines of a divine triangle, sealed at a fourth center.

steps.label: Canon of the sanctuary
steps.note: Nature and Scripture joined in Christ, living in the believer.

slides.notes: Franckenberg, friend and biographer of Jacob Böhme, republished the Clavis through Ioannem Jansonius, with a dedication to Werner of Pallant and an appendix, Key of the Key. Concord, he says, comes by the tenuous breath of grace, not by war or dogma. The chain he names: Joachim of Fiore, Pico della Mirandola, Reuchlin, Agrippa, Francesco Giorgio, Giordano Bruno, Julius Sperber. His phrase: Writing with Nature and Nature with Writing.

slides.title: Seventy-eight, by the Name
slides.evidence: Four suits of fourteen make the 56 Minor Arcana. Twenty-one numbered trumps and one unnumbered card make the 22 Major.
slides.implication: Commentators who cite Postel's Clavis and Lévi govern that pack by Yod-He-Vau-He.
slides.notes: The briefing calls this a mechanical apparatus of strict numerical laws. It attributes the system to esoteric analyses referencing the Clavis and Lévi's Dogme et Rituel, and Papus's Tarot of the Bohemians in the closing table. It does not say Postel designed the cards.

slides.title: Four figures, one name
slides.notes: Each suit is four figures and ten numbers, Ace through Ten. The second He is the transition term. The briefing calls the Knight neuter as well as adolescent.

slides.title: The ten, across three worlds

points.label: Divine world
points.note: Emanation: 1, 2, 3, 4. The King, with aces, twos, and threes. The head.

points.label: Human world
points.note: Evolution: 4, 5, 6, 7. The Queen, with fours, fives, and sixes. The chest.

points.label: Material world
points.note: Evolution: 7, 8, 9, 10. The Knight, with sevens, eights, and nines. The body.

points.label: The transition
points.note: The Knave holds the tens, and passes the suit on toward the Major Arcana.

slides.notes: The briefing links the worlds by repeating 4 and 7, and calls the ten the transition term. The material series includes 10, while the anatomy gives the tens to the Knave rather than the Knight. Both statements are kept.

slides.title: Suits, letters, and vessels
slides.notes: Principles in the briefing: Sceptre, male and active; Cup, female and passive; Sword, union and the crucial form; Pentacle, the transition term, from natural to supernatural. The Pentacles, the second He, bridge the 56 Minor Arcana to the 22 Major Arcana.

slides.title: Three epochs of the Rose

epochs.label: Paracelsian reform
epochs.note: Fama, Confessio, and the Chymical Wedding, Tübingen and Kassel.

epochs.label: Stuart restoration
epochs.note: Moray, Erskine, and Ashmole, in the networks for the Stuarts.

epochs.label: High-grade revival
epochs.note: Golden and Rosy Cross, Richter, Oetinger, then Herder and Hegel.

slides.notes: The briefing defines Rosicrucianism as an invisible, non-organizational Christian-Hermetic theosophy: spiritual knights keeping a feminine flame, Sophia or the Shekhinah, a rose outside and the blue fire of alchemy within. The Fama places C.R.C.'s learning in Damcar. The 1615 Frankfurt Confessio corrects that name to Damar, a city in Yemen. Precursors named here: Simon Studion's Naometria (1592) and Cruce Signata (1586); Dee's Monas, explicated by Gabella in 1615; Khunrath's Amphitheatrum.

slides.title: Two readings of the same rose

left.title: Astro-spiritual
points: Gabella, Michael Maier, and Robert Fludd.
Dee's Monas, Ssabian temples, and alchemical tinctures.
Angelic magic, of macrocosm and microcosm.

right.title: Pietist
points: Johann Valentin Andreae and Melchior Breler.
Tauler, Thomas à Kempis, and Johann Arndt.
Inward regeneration, and the devotional cross.

slides.notes: The briefing calls the right-hand camp Pietist and Lutheran, and traces it to German mysticism. Damar, in the Confessio, is also offered as a government of wise men and a model for European reform. The esoteric gloss of Damcar is blood of the Lamb.

slides.title: Monas, rune, Adulruna
slides.caption: In 1610 Bureus set Dee's Monas on the rune Bjarkan. The Adulruna is a crucified sun in an infinite circle. He read the Northern runes as Skanzea's script.
slides.notes: Bureus, 1568–1652, archivist and tutor to Gustav II Adolf. A diagram header gives a death year before the birth. The prose and the closing table say 1568–1652, which this deck uses. The Japhetic line is from Postel's De Originibus: Noah, Japheth, Gomer, Askenaz, then Skanzea. The Monas was a 1564 copy from the Jesuit library at Posen. Manuals in 1611 and 1643. Pamphlets: Ara Foederis Therapici and FaMa e sCanzIa reDUX (1616), then Surge (1622). Bjarkan is paired with Aries.

slides.title: Three crowns, three gods

items.label: Thor, the Father
items.note: Lumen and divine law. Jupiter, and Thora as the law of the Jews.

items.label: Othin, the Son
items.note: Verbum Dei and sapientia. Mars and Hercules, the eternal word.

items.label: Freya, Holy Spirit
items.note: Divine goodness and fecundity. The Ephesian Diana.

slides.notes: Bureus claims Uppsala was founded before Abraham. The three golden crowns stand for three fylkelands, Tyunda, Ottunda, and Ferugra, and for these three gods. He calls Zamolxes and Abaris northern sages who taught Pythagoras, and he dates the sibyl Alruna to 432 BC.

slides.title: The meadows are full
slides.quote: Close up the streams, young boy, for the meadows have drunk themselves full
slides.attribution: Virgil, Eclogues III, as heard by Bureus
slides.source: Stora Tuna, Dalecarlia, 6:30 in the morning
slides.notes: The singing voice gave the line in capitals, RIVos IaM CLaVDe PVEr sat prata bIberVnt, whose numeral letters Bureus read as 1673. He drew a crucified heart with three nails, inscribed ECCe CRVCeM Cor et ClaVos IesV, which he read as 1666. He took the pair as the opening of the scroll with seven seals in Revelations 5:5, the secret that no author could disclose.

slides.title: The Lion of the North

left.title: The prophecy
points: Paracelsus forecasts a northern chemical liberator.
Roeslin and Paul Grebner expand the forecast.
The name in German: der Löwe aus der Mitternacht.

right.title: The Swedish crown
points: Taken up by the crown and the Protestant League, 1630–1632.
Bureus names Gustav II Adolf the anointed liberator.
An Erfurt coin of 1633 shows him with sulphur and mercury.

slides.notes: Bureus says Gustav II Adolf will crush Apap, the papal antichrist and dragon, and open a seventh age of peace. The briefing's parenthetical dates for Helisaeus Roeslin are impossible and are left off this slide. Roeslin remains the author of Theoria Nova Meteoron (1578), on the 1572 Cassiopeia supernova, writing as Lampertus Floridus.

slides.title: Five systems, one argument
slides.notes: Cells are compressed from the briefing's closing table so each one can sit on a slide. The Rosicrucian row keeps the first-epoch date the table itself uses. Later epochs are on the timeline. Bureus's aim in the source is Hyperborean Gothic supremacy and the verification of Gustav Adolf as the Lion of the North.

slides.title: How to hold the briefing
slides.prompt: Hold each system as its author's claim. The Tarot map cites Postel and Lévi. The 1615 Confessio corrects Damcar to Damar in Yemen.
slides.notes: Damar was a Sabean center in Yemen, linked in the briefing to the Queen of Sheba. The Ssabians of Harran, often conflated there with the Mandaeans, built planetary temples: triangle for Jupiter, square for the Sun, hexagon in a square for Mercury. Esoterically the briefing glosses Damcar as blood of the Lamb, a cover for the place-name Damar.
